name: David Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly it's the bus and the lecture hall. I'm doing computer science, and I live at home with my mum in a two-bed flat, so I'm up at six to get the bus in. Three days a week I have lectures and labs, and on Saturdays and Sundays I stack shelves at a big supermarket distribution site for about fourteen hours total. The labs are my favourite part, even though I'm slower than the lads who've been coding since they were twelve.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What would you least like to lose from that week?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The Thursday lab, honestly. We write small programs in pairs, and my lab partner, Tomasz, explains things without making me feel stupid. I got in on good grades but I didn't grow up with a laptop of my own, so I'm learning the basics from scratch. If I lost that lab I'd lose the only place where I feel like I belong on the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd say fine, good, because I never believed the hype. I'd tell my mates that these tools are overrated and the people selling them want shares to go up. At the warehouse we already have scanners that tell us what to pick, and nobody lost a job over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel relieved but not safe. My loan covers fees, and I've got under a month of living costs saved, so a normal world is still a tight world. If AI doesn't change much then the jobs I'm training for just stay scarce and badly paid at the bottom, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am: lectures, Saturday and Sunday shifts, and I'd try to pick up a second weekday evening shift if the warehouse offers one. I'd put aside about twenty pounds a week for the rent my mum asks me to chip in. I wouldn't touch any AI tools, because I want to understand the code I write myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. It feels like nothing changes and I'm still the one running to keep up. There's a bit of relief, but money worry doesn't go away just because the robots stay in the movies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the world carries on as normal. What would still keep you up at night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Debt, and my mum's hours. She cleans offices and her boss cut her shifts last spring, so even if AI turns out to be nothing, my mum and I are still one bad month away from missing the rent. I'd watch her face when the post comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any of the AI tools your classmates mention?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't, and I get stick for it. Tomasz uses one to explain errors and he says it saves him hours. I'd rather stay stuck for an hour and actually learn it, because if the exam is on paper I'll need it in my head.

say: I'd say the hype is oversold and **nothing** much changes for ordinary people.
I'd tell mates the firms selling AI just want **share prices** up.
think: I feel relieved but not safe, because **debt** and thin savings stay either way.
Entry-level tech jobs stay **scarce** and badly paid, the same as now.
do: Keep up lectures and the **weekend shifts** at the distribution site.
Ask for a second **evening shift** to chip in on mum's rent.
Avoid AI tools and learn the code by hand.
feel: **Tired** and running to keep up, with only a little relief.
S0.quote: even if AI turns out to be nothing, my mum and I are still one bad month away from missing the rent
fieldNote: **Money worry** is already high; he sees no change as no escape from rent and loans.
Strong **distrust** of AI firms, shaped by watching mum's cleaning hours get cut.
Honest that he doesn't use **AI** on purpose, and takes teasing for it.

steps.text: Keep working the weekend shifts at the distribution site
Put aside twenty pounds a week towards mum's rent
Ask the university hardship fund about a small grant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be companies cutting corners and calling it progress. If AI takes over writing, checking and coding, then the people at the bottom, like grads and part-timers, get squeezed first. I'd say we need rules and unions involved before it spreads, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm scared that the exact job I'm studying for is the one that gets chewed up. My course is mostly coding, and coding is on the card. If firms stop hiring juniors because software does the easy tasks, I don't know who gives me a first job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my course tutor which modules are still going to matter and lean harder on the maths and the networking ones. I'd join the student union's campaign group, because I think collective pressure is the only thing that works. And I'd still avoid the AI tools for now, though I'd probably have to try one eventually, grudgingly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit angry, if I'm honest. It feels like the rules get written by people who already have money, and I'm told to adapt quickly. I keep thinking of my mum, who can't adapt out of cleaning, because it's cleaning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame in that picture, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big firms and the people who make them richer. I don't blame the tools, I blame bosses who use them to avoid paying people. If a company saves millions by replacing juniors, it should pay into a fund that supports the people it displaced, and I'd vote for whoever says that out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your tutor tell you to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably 'learn everything', which isn't an answer. I think they'd say pick up the AI tools, and I'd feel stubborn about it. I'd probably still check if the university can give me a placement, because experience is harder to automate than a CV.

say: I'd say firms will use AI to **cut corners** and squeeze juniors first.
I'd say we need **rules** and unions in place before it spreads.
think: The coding I'm studying is **exactly** what gets chewed up first.
If firms stop hiring juniors, I don't know who gives me a **first job**.
do: Ask my tutor which **modules** still matter and lean on maths and networking.
Look for a university **placement** for real experience.
feel: **Angry** that rules get written by people who already have money.
S1.quote: If a company saves millions by replacing juniors, it should pay into a fund that supports the people it displaced
fieldNote: Blames **employers**, not the technology, and wants unions and a displacement fund.
Sees his own **course** as directly exposed, which is rare among first-years who talk only in general terms.
Resists AI tools out of **stubbornness**, though he knows he may have to try one.

steps.text: Join the student union campaign group on jobs and AI
Vote for parties that back a displaced-workers fund
Ask the tutor about a placement year in second year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disaster in the making and no government will be ready. Two years isn't enough to rewrite a law, let alone retrain millions. I'd say it online too, probably, though I'm not great at posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think I've started a degree that might be pointless before I finish it. I'm in first year, so I'd get maybe a year of study and then the very job I'd be applying for is gone. And my mum's cleaning job might hold longer than my degree, which is a strange thing to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably talk to my mum about whether to keep paying fees on a loan, and ask the university if I could pause. I'd look for any steady job I can do with my hands, like warehouse work, while it's still there, because robots are 3 years behind the thinking AI. I'd also go to every union meeting I could and push for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, kind of. My stomach would drop each time I looked at the loan letter. I'd feel like a kid who was told study hard and now the rules changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit at the kitchen table and say we need to stop thinking in four-year plans. I'd tell my mum we should save every pound we can now, because the plan we had stops working in two years. She'd probably cry and say I should finish my degree anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about 3 years after. Does that change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, it gives the warehouse about five years total, so I'd stay there and take more shifts instead of leaving. But I wouldn't trust that, because the warehouse already runs on scanners and the managers would automate the second they could. It's a thin bridge.

say: I'd say **two years** isn't enough for any government to be ready.
I'd say it **online** too, though I'm not much of a poster.
think: My degree might be **pointless** before I finish it.
Mum's cleaning job could outlast my **degree**, which is a strange thing to say.
do: Ask the university if I can **pause** my course and loan.
Take more **warehouse** shifts, since robots arrive about three years later.
Attend every union meeting and push for a **basic income**.
feel: **Sick**, like my stomach drops each time the loan letter arrives.
S2.quote: I'd tell my mum we should save every pound we can now, because the plan we had stops working in two years
fieldNote: Expects the **degree** to lose value mid-course, so the loan feels like a trap.
Treats the **3-year** robot gap as a thin bridge for warehouse work, and doesn't trust it.
Talks first about his **mum**, whose income is also at risk.

steps.text: Ask the university whether I can pause my course and loan
Save every spare pound towards mum's rent
Go to union meetings and push for basic income
Write to my MP asking for a retraining guarantee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but at least people can see it. I'd tell mates to stop treating it as sci-fi and start asking what they'd do if their job vanished. I'd say the government should start now, not in year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I finish my degree just as it lands, with loans in my pocket and nothing to show. I'm 18 now, so I'd be 23 when the thinking AI is meant to be here. It's like running toward a door and knowing it's closing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd finish the degree year and try to land a summer job at a firm that does infrastructure or engineering, something with a physical side. I'd learn a trade skill on the side, like electrics, through a weekend course if I could afford it. I'd also join the union drive and ask for the university to teach what survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit angry. There's time, which helps, but nobody is using it. I picture my mum saying it'll be fine and I don't believe her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the physical side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the card says robots come three years later, and that's a gap I can use. A trade like electrics gives me a few extra years of work, and it's something my mum could be proud of. I'd rather be a qualified electrician with a computer science year behind me than a coder with a loan and no job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do any of that differently if you'd had the warning from the start of school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd have picked an apprenticeship at the start. But I wanted the degree because nobody in my family went to university. It's a feeling more than a plan, and I'd have to admit that.

say: I'd say five years is tight but people can still **see it coming**.
I'd say the government should start **now**, not in year four.
think: I'd finish my degree just as it lands, with **loans** and little to show.
It's like running toward a **door** I know is closing.
do: Look for a summer job with a physical side in **engineering**.
Take a weekend **electrics** course if I can afford it.
Join the union drive and ask the university to teach what **survives**.
feel: **Uneasy** and angry, because nobody is using the warning time.
S3.quote: I'd rather be a qualified electrician with a computer science year behind me than a coder with a loan and no job
fieldNote: Uses the **3-year** robot gap deliberately to justify a hands-on fallback.
Admits the **degree** is partly about family pride, as nobody before him went to university.
**Anger** is aimed at institutions that waste warning time.

steps.text: Look for a summer job at an engineering firm with site work
Take a weekend electrics course next spring
Join the union drive on AI and graduate jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth and last picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do something if people actually do it. I'd tell mates that we should be pushing for retraining funds and rules while we're young. I'd probably say it with more energy than I feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I feel a bit better about ten years, because I'd be 28 and could have a career and savings before it hits. But I know my mum is closer to the edge, because she'd be near sixty, and cleaning may fall to robots a few years after the thinking work. I worry more about her than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, take a placement year, and try to get a proper graduate job quickly so I can build a cushion. I'd pay down the loan as fast as I can and maybe help my mum move into something less physical. I'd try an AI tool at some point, because ten years is long enough that avoiding it would be silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but with a little guilt. I'd feel guilty planning my own career when my mum's job is the one at risk. Ten years feels like breathing room, if I use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for your mum in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Help her get a certificate in something like care work or building maintenance, where she'd have a few more years. I'd rather spend my first good salary getting my mum out of cleaning than buying anything for myself. That's what ten years should be for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you trust the ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not completely. People always say there's time and then it comes quicker. I'd keep a bit of money untouched in case it speeds up.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough** if people actually act.
I'd push for **retraining** funds and rules while we're young.
think: Ten years lets me build a career and **savings** before it hits.
I worry more about **mum**, since cleaning may fall to robots soon after.
do: Finish the degree, take a **placement** year, and aim for a graduate job.
Pay down the **loan** fast and build a cushion.
Help mum get a **certificate** in a less physical field.
feel: **Calmer**, with some guilt about planning my career while mum's job is at risk.
S4.quote: I'd rather spend my first good salary getting my mum out of cleaning than buying anything for myself
fieldNote: **Ten years** eases his own fear but not his mum's, which keeps the mood from dropping further.
Starts to soften on **AI tools** once the timeline is long enough.
Keeps a **reserve** because he doesn't trust timelines.

steps.text: Take a placement year and aim for a graduate job
Pay extra off the loan every month after graduating
Help mum find a care or maintenance certificate
Try one AI coding tool in third year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. Two years is nothing, and my mum and I would have no cushion, no plan, and a loan with my name on it. What would help is a real guarantee, like retraining paid for and a job promise for people who lose theirs, and a say for unions in how firms bring this in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I don't think I'm against AI, I'm against being left behind by it. People think I'm stubborn for not using the tools. I'd rather be the person who understands the code than the person who's told what to type.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be the person who understands the code than the person who's told what to type
portrait: David is an **18-year-old** computer science first-year who lives with his mum and stacks shelves at weekends.
He is **progressive**, distrusts big tech and employers, and wants unions and rules in place before change spreads.
He never uses AI tools, partly out of principle and partly because he's still learning the basics.
He shares his **worry** with his mum, a cleaner whose hours were cut, and plans around her too.
He moves from tired and anxious to **alarmed** when time is short, and eases a little with ten years.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries him most, because two years leaves no cushion and no plan.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **retraining** paid for, a job guarantee, and unions involved in how firms adopt AI.
